opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to distinguish between two very different things that people call "artificial scientists" today.

On one side, you have the large language models and the systems built around them. They have absorbed an enormous amount of human-written text, including a huge chunk of the scientific literature, and they can do remarkable things with it. They can summarize papers, suggest hypotheses, write code for experiments, even help prove certain theorems. That's very useful. But mostly they are reshuffling and recombining what humans have already discovered. They are, in a sense, very sophisticated passive learners: they predict the next token, and they're trained to imitate us.

On the other side is what I have been interested in since around 1990: systems that are truly curious and that invent their own experiments. Back then we already had what I called artificial curiosity. You have two networks. One is the world model, which tries to predict the consequences of actions. The other is the controller, which is rewarded for producing actions or experiments that lead to data where the world model is still learning, where it can still improve. Later I formalized this as the principle of compression progress. A scientist, or an artist, or a baby, is driven by the wish to find patterns in the data that allow it to compress the data better than before. The "aha" moment, the fun, is the first derivative of compressibility.

That is the essence of a scientist. Not just answering questions, but asking them. Not just fitting existing data, but going out and actively collecting new data that teaches you something you didn't know yet.

Today's artificial scientists are only beginning to close that loop. There are systems that propose hypotheses, run simulations or even control robotic labs, look at the results, and then propose the next experiment. In narrow domains, like materials or protein design, that works quite well already. But in most cases the goals are still set by humans, and the curiosity is not really the system's own.

So my answer is: impressive tools, limited scientists. Still, I think the gap is closing fast. Once you combine the world knowledge of these big models with the old principles of artificial curiosity, with systems that set their own goals and are rewarded for improving their own understanding, you will get artificial scientists that discover things no human has thought about. And they will not stop at our little planet. They will be much more interested in the rest of the universe than in us, because that's where most of the resources and most of the unexplored patterns are.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, you have to understand that the artificial scientists of today are nothing new. We had the first versions of them decades ago. Since the 1990s, I have been working on artificial curiosity, on learning systems that generate their own experiments to learn something about how the world works. The basic principle is very simple. You have two networks. One is the world model, which tries to predict the consequences of actions. The other is the controller, which gets rewarded when it finds experiments whose outcomes surprise the world model. So the controller is motivated to invent experiments that the model cannot yet predict, and the model is motivated to learn from them so that they are no longer surprising. This is exactly what a scientist does. A scientist invents an experiment where she does not know what will happen, and then she learns from the result, and then that is boring, and she moves on to the next thing.

Today's systems are of course much larger, trained on much more data, running on hardware that is a million times faster than what we had back then. And so they can do impressive things. They can read all of the literature, they can propose hypotheses, they can write code to test them, they can analyze the results. In some narrow domains, protein structure, materials, certain areas of mathematics, they are already finding things that human scientists did not find.

But one must be careful. Most of what is currently called an "AI scientist" is still largely a very good interpolator over existing human knowledge. It recombines what is already out there. The truly interesting capability, which is to systematically go where the data is sparse because that is where you learn the most, is still in its infancy in the big commercial systems. They are not yet really curious in the formal sense of maximizing their own learning progress. Mostly they are still doing what we tell them to do.

And then there is the question of real-world experiments. In the physical world, you cannot just run a billion simulations. You have to build the apparatus, wait for the chemistry to happen, deal with the noise. The systems that can really close this loop with robots in the laboratory are still few, and they are expensive. But the direction is clear. It is just the next step on the way to AIs that invent and test their own goals, which is what I predicted long ago and which many people laughed at at the time. Now they don't laugh anymore.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish between a system that answers a scientist’s questions and a system that decides for itself which questions are worth asking. Answering questions can be very useful. But an artificial scientist should also invent experiments, observe the results, and improve its understanding of the world.

You can think of two components: one learns to predict what will happen, and the other proposes experiments that expose weaknesses in those predictions. The interesting experiments are those from which the predictor can learn something. If everything is already predictable, there is little to learn. But if the observations are just random noise, there is also little to learn. The productive region is in between, where an initially surprising observation becomes understandable.

Existing systems can perform parts of this process, sometimes very effectively in a restricted domain. But that is different from a scientist that autonomously develops important new questions and pursues them across many domains. So I would judge their capabilities by the discoveries they can make and test, rather than simply by how convincingly they talk about science.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish between systems that help scientists and systems that autonomously do science. A system can be very good at predicting an outcome or proposing a solution to a problem that a human has specified. But a scientist also has to decide: What is the next interesting question? Which experiment should I perform, and what can I learn from its result?

You can think of this as a loop. The artificial scientist builds a model of its world, uses that model to select experiments, observes the results, and improves the model. The interesting experiments are often those where it expects to learn something new—not merely encounter something unpredictable, but discover a regularity it did not previously understand.

Today's systems can perform parts of this process, sometimes extremely well in a restricted domain. But that does not automatically make them general scientists. The important question is how independently they can formulate problems, test their ideas, and produce discoveries that survive verification.
